title: Pay Attention, Be Astonished
author: The Walled Garden
summary: In the third installment of a six-part series on attention as curriculum, The Walled Garden argues that classrooms fail to teach attention well not because they lack technique, but because they rarely name what attention should be directed toward. Drawing on Buddhaghosa's fifth-century Visuddhimagga, which catalogues forty different meditation objects all serving one fixed aim, liberation from suffering, the author establishes that every serious attentional tradition pairs a flexible object with a deliberately chosen, non-negotiable purpose. The piece then uses historian Jamie Kreiner's account of medieval monastic life, and the monks' concept of acedia, a spiritual paralysis caused by an untethered mind, to show that undirected attention has long been treated as a serious threat rather than a minor productivity lapse. Its central contrast is between institutions that choose their aim on purpose, like the monks, and institutions that inherit an aim by default, like social media platforms optimizing for engagement or classrooms that default to compliance and grades when no explicit aim is named. The essay closes by proposing concrete subject-level aims, history toward recognizing perspective, math toward logic, literature toward empathy, and lands on Mary Oliver's instruction to pay attention, be astonished, and tell about it as a description of what teaching itself actually is: naming what deserves attention and modeling astonishment at it.
points: The author argues, using Buddhism's forty catalogued meditation objects as an example, that every serious attentional tradition pairs a flexible object of focus with a fixed, deliberately chosen aim, and that classrooms rarely name an aim at all.

Citing Jamie Kreiner's history of medieval monastic life, the piece uses acedia, the monks' term for spiritual paralysis from an untethered mind, to argue that undirected attention has always been treated as a serious threat.

The core contrast is between institutions that choose their aim deliberately (monks) and institutions that inherit an aim by default (social media platforms optimizing for engagement, and classrooms defaulting to compliance).
Concrete subject-level examples, history aiming at perspective, math at logic, literature at empathy, show what it looks like for a teacher to name a real aim instead of a vague 'engagement' goal.
The piece's payoff is Mary Oliver's three-part instruction (pay attention, be astonished, tell about it), used to argue teaching itself is the act of naming what's worth attending to.
quotes: Every tradition that has taken attention seriously has answered that question the same way: not by leaving it undirected, but by choosing, deliberately, what it should be for.
But focusing on one's breath is only the proximate object. Regardless of what you're assigned, Buddhism has a universal, non-negotiable aim: liberation from suffering.

The investor Charlie Munger had a line for this: "Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome." Tristan Harris has spent years tracking what that principle produces in social media platforms built to hold your attention.

Their word for the danger of an untethered mind was acedia — a kind of spiritual paralysis that could leave a monk unable to summon the will to pray, work, or do much of anything else. A wandering mind was more than a lapse in productivity; it was threatening to the whole purpose of a monk's life.

Silicon Valley optimizes for an incentive it inherited, not one it chose. Profit-from-attention came from the market; their engineers are tasked with chasing it. The monks chose their object first, then built around it.

When the aim goes unnamed, our students default to the system's incentives. Their aim becomes compliance — achievement, competition, a grade. An aim revealed by default requires no reflection, no consideration, and no critical thought.
